content: Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is a critical treatment for patients with end-stage kidney disease, utilized by over 200,000 individuals worldwide. However, its effectiveness is often compromised by infections, including peritonitis, as well as exit-site and tunnel infections. Various strategies have been developed to mitigate the risk of peritonitis, such as the use of antibiotics, topical disinfectants at the catheter exit site, and antifungal agents. Despite these efforts, the effectiveness of these interventions has been inconsistent, as they are often based on a limited number of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The optimal approach to prevent peritonitis in PD patients remains uncertain. This review is an update of a Cochrane review initially published in 2004. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and potential harms of antimicrobial strategies aimed at preventing peritonitis in patients undergoing PD. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Specialised Register up to October 4, 2016. The search included studies identified through CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, conference proceedings, and clinical trial registries. The review included RCTs and quasi-RCTs that evaluated systemic or local antimicrobial agents for the prevention of peritonitis or exit-site/tunnel infections in chronic PD patients. A total of 39 studies involving 4,435 patients were included in this review, with 20 additional studies added since the previous update. The quality of the studies varied, with many demonstrating unclear or high risk of bias. For example, only 49% of studies had low risk of bias in random sequence generation, 31% in allocation concealment, 56% in incomplete outcome reporting, and 31% in selective outcome reporting. Blinding of participants and personnel was often not feasible due to the nature of the interventions, and only 21% of studies had low risk of bias in this domain. The use of oral or topical antibiotics compared to placebo or no treatment showed uncertain effects on reducing the risk of exit-site/tunnel infections (3 studies, 191 patients; low-quality evidence: risk ratio [RR] 0.45, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.19 to 1.04) and peritonitis (5 studies, 395 patients; low-quality evidence: RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.19). Similarly, nasal antibiotics aimed at eradicating Staphylococcus aureus had uncertain effects on the risk of exit-site/tunnel infections (3 studies, 338 patients; low-quality evidence: RR 1.34, 95% CI 0.62 to 2.87) and peritonitis (3 studies, 338 patients; low-quality evidence: RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.31). Preor perioperative intravenous vancomycin, when compared to no treatment, may reduce the risk of early peritonitis (1 study, 177 patients; low-quality evidence: RR 0.08, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.61). However, its effect on exit-site/tunnel infections remains uncertain (1 study, 177 patients; low-quality evidence: RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.10 to 1.32). The use of topical disinfectants compared to standard care or other active treatments (e.g., antibiotics or other disinfectants) also showed uncertain effects on the risk of exit-site/tunnel infections (8 studies, 973 patients; low-quality evidence: RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.33) and peritonitis (6 studies, 853 patients; low-quality evidence: RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.06). Antifungal prophylaxis with oral nystatin or fluconazole, when compared to placebo or no treatment, may reduce the risk of fungal peritonitis following a course of antibiotics (2 studies, 817 patients; low-quality evidence: RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.63). However, no intervention demonstrated a significant reduction in the need for catheter removal or replacement. Most of the included studies were small and of suboptimal quality, with only six studies enrolling 200 or more patients. This highlights the lack of adequately powered and high-quality RCTs in this area. In conclusion, this review found limited evidence from RCTs and quasi-RCTs evaluating strategies to prevent peritonitis and exit-site/tunnel infections in PD patients. Preor perioperative intravenous vancomycin may reduce the risk of early peritonitis, and antifungal prophylaxis with oral nystatin or fluconazole may lower the risk of fungal peritonitis following antibiotic use. However, no other antimicrobial interventions demonstrated clear efficacy. The uncertain effects of nasal antibiotics in preventing peritonitis raise questions about their utility. Given the large number of patients undergoing PD and the significant impact of peritonitis, the lack of robust, high-quality RCTs to guide preventive strategies is a critical gap in the evidence base.
